co_riviera_the.blurb: A single-pitch granite wall on the canyon road west of Boulder, roughly seven miles up, sitting just downhill of the Bihedral. Around two dozen lines are spread along a face about two hundred feet wide, with trad climbs outnumbering bolted ones about two to one. Grades start at 5.6 and climb past 5.12, but the bulk fall between 5.7 and 5.10, so it suits climbers working through the middle grades. Expect textured, quartzy granite with a mix of cracks, slabs and steeper jug pulls. The wall faces south, which makes it pleasant in cooler months and warm in summer. Popular near town, so groups can crowd the wall on good days.

co_first_flatiron.blurb: The First Flatiron is a huge tilted slab on the hillside above Boulder, and its east face holds long traditional lines of roughly four to ten pitches. About twenty routes are catalogued, all trad, and most are moderate: easy low-fifth and scrambling-grade terrain through the mid fives and sixes, with a few harder lines and a single 5.11. A 60 m rope helps with the rappels. The walk from the Chautauqua trailhead takes 20 to 40 minutes. Face climbing, big flakes and dihedrals make nearly every line worthwhile, and the popularity shows, so expect company on good days.

co_second_flatiron.blurb: The Second Flatiron stands between the First and Third in the Boulder foothills, and it is quieter than its neighbors. Most of the roughly twenty climbs are long trad scrambles and slab routes of several pitches, with easy low-grade lines alongside a handful of 5.6 to 5.9 pitches and one hard 5.11. A few boulder problems sit at the base, ranging from very easy to quite hard, and there is one aid line. The hike in from Chautauqua takes about half an hour. The slabs are steep and exposed for their grade, and the face looks west, so plan on afternoon sun.

co_seurat_area.blurb: A high-elevation boulder field, near 11,000 feet, scattered through forest a little south of the Bierstadt boulders, inside the wilderness around Mt Blue Sky (the peak once called Mount Evans). About two dozen granite problems range from V1 up to V12, with a sizable cluster in the V3 to V5 range and a hard tail of tall, demanding lines. The standouts are a classic lieback crack, two long arete traverses and several highballs that need multiple pads. Tree cover makes it a sensible pick on warm days. Weather turns quickly at this altitude, and the walk in is long.

co_firehouse_area.blurb: A cliff band in the East Vail neighborhood, near 8,800 feet, split into east and west sections. Winter brings steep, short water ice from WI2 up to WI5, and a dozen of the climbs are ice, with a similar number of drytooling lines on pink limestone and sandstone that run from M5 into the M8 range. Many of the ice routes are concentrated around WI5, so this is better for confident leaders than for first-timers. The flows are shorter than those at the neighboring Designator wall, but the steepness makes up for it. Reach the base by trail and then a steep gully of a couple hundred feet.

co_fiddlehead.blurb: A freestanding rock on the north side of Fern Canyon in the southern Flatirons above Boulder, around 7,250 feet. Twenty-odd routes mix trad and sport, and the character changes by side: the east face holds a long, easy 5.4 line, while the steeper west face carries the hard sport climbs, with many pitches from the 5.10s through 5.13. Some routes run two pitches. It is reached on foot via the Mesa Trail and the Fern Canyon path, followed by a short off-trail scramble to the east face, and the south end is broken and overgrown, so finding the base takes care.

co_little_big_man_area.blurb: A small section of the Quarry Wall in Unaweep Canyon, near Grand Junction, at about 7,000 feet. Roughly two dozen short granite routes mostly follow cracks, with trad lines making up over half, plus top-rope climbs and a few bolted ones. Grades run from 5.6 to 5.12, centered on the 5.9 to 5.10 range, with cracks of varied width including chimneys, fists and flaring hand cracks. The wall stays out of the sun until well into the afternoon, which makes it a decent summer option. Rock quality can switch from solid to blocky, so test holds.
